en.title: Education English: the whole course
en.short: What Education English covers, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Education English is the study of two things together: the English language and literature, and the craft of teaching them. It prepares teachers for schools, colleges and other learning settings. One half asks what English is: how sounds, words, sentences and meanings work; how literature works; how people acquire and learn languages. The other half asks how to teach it: how learners develop, how curricula are built, how lessons are planned, how learning is assessed, and how classrooms are managed. The two halves must connect. A teacher who knows grammar but cannot explain it to a mixed class is not yet prepared, and a teacher who knows methods but not the subject will run out of content.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text: Degrees differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a bachelor’s degree in education is commonly a four-year programme. The award may be B.Ed, B.Sc.(Ed) or B.A.(Ed), depending on the university and the subject combination. English Education may sit inside a Faculty or College of Education. Programmes usually include general education courses, professional education courses, subject courses and teaching practice. The National Universities Commission (NUC) regulates university programmes, and the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) registers teachers, but requirements change. In Ghana, education degrees are also common, with their own structure and regulator. In the United Kingdom, teacher preparation may be a degree with qualified teacher status or a postgraduate route. Do not assume that one country’s length, title or licence applies in another.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Start with the introductory stage. Language and Linguistics: Foundations for English Teachers gives the map. English Phonetics and Phonology, English Morphology and Syntax, and Semantics and Pragmatics build the language description you will teach. Introduction to Literary Studies opens the study of texts. Language Acquisition and Learning explains how languages are learned. Educational Psychology for Teachers, Curriculum Foundations and Introduction to English Education connect subject knowledge to schooling.

The core stage turns this into classroom practice. Teaching Listening and Speaking, Teaching Reading and Comprehension, Teaching Writing and Composition, Teaching Grammar and Vocabulary, and Teaching Literature are the methods courses. Children’s and Adolescent Literature, African Literature in English and Survey of English Literature widen your literary base. Sociolinguistics and World Englishes helps you treat English as a world language. English Curriculum and Lesson Planning, Assessment in English Education, Instructional Materials and ICT, Classroom Management, Inclusive Education and Professional Ethics for Teachers cover professional decisions. Microteaching and Teaching Practice give supervised rehearsal, and Research Methods in English Education introduces inquiry.

At master’s level, Theories of Second Language Acquisition, Advanced Research Methods in English Education, Critical Literacy and Multimodality, and Language Policy and Planning in Education deepen theory and research.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study the subject and the teaching together. For language, practise description: transcribe a short phrase, parse a sentence, explain a meaning in plain words. For literature, read the text before reading summaries, and keep a page of notes on theme, form and context. For education, turn theory into a lesson: take one concept and plan how you would teach it to a named class.

Use microteaching and teaching practice as feedback, not performance. Ask for comments on clarity, pace, questioning and checking understanding. Keep a file of lesson plans, materials and reflections. Read official curriculum documents for your country and level, because syllabuses and examinations differ. Check current requirements with your institution and regulator.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include studying English and education as separate boxes. Students may know a grammar rule but not how to teach it, or know a method but not enough content. Another mistake is treating one country’s curriculum, examination or licence as universal. Always name the country and check the current official source.

In literature, students sometimes use summaries instead of reading. In methods, they plan activities without a clear learning aim. In assessment, they confuse a test score with learning. In teaching practice, they cover content too fast and do not check understanding. In research, they make claims beyond their data. Keep your claims modest and your evidence clear.

keyPoints: Education English joins subject knowledge in English with professional knowledge of teaching.
Degrees, awards and licence rules differ by country, so check your own handbook and regulator.
The introductory stage builds language, literature, psychology and curriculum foundations.
The core stage turns these into methods, materials, assessment, management and supervised practice.
Study subject and method together, and use teaching practice as feedback.
Name the country for any curriculum, examination or law, and check current official sources.

en.title: Language and Linguistics: Foundations for English Teachers
en.short: What language is, the levels of linguistic analysis, key branches, and English as a world language.

sections.heading: What language is
sections.text:
Language is a system of arbitrary symbols that a community uses to communicate and to think. Arbitrary means the sound of a word does not copy its meaning. Two features matter for teachers: language is rule-governed (users share a grammar) and creative (a speaker can produce sentences never heard before).

Linguistics is its systematic study; it describes use rather than prescribing rules. That difference matters in the classroom. A teacher who knows the rule can explain why a form is non-standard instead of only marking it wrong.

sections.heading: Levels of analysis
sections.text:
Linguists divide language into levels. Phonetics studies speech sounds as physical events; phonology studies the sound system, that is, which sounds contrast in a language. Morphology studies word structure, syntax studies how words combine into phrases and sentences, semantics studies literal meaning, and pragmatics studies meaning in context, including what is implied but not said.

Each level gives a teacher a name for a learner’s problem. If a pupil writes "My father have two car", the teacher can point to syntax (subject-verb agreement) and morphology (the missing plural -s).

sections.heading: Branches of linguistics
sections.text: Branches link language to other questions. Sociolinguistics studies language and society: regional and social variation, register, and attitudes to accents. Psycholinguistics studies how the mind produces and understands language. Historical linguistics studies change over time. Applied linguistics uses linguistic findings to solve practical problems, especially language teaching, dictionary making and language policy. English teaching sits mainly within applied linguistics.

sections.heading: English as a world language
sections.text:
English is used worldwide, and most of its speakers learnt it as a second or additional language. Braj Kachru’s often cited model groups users into three circles: inner (countries where English is a first language, such as the United Kingdom and the United States), outer (countries such as Nigeria, India and Kenya, where it has official and institutional roles) and expanding (countries such as China, where it is learnt mainly as a foreign language).

The model is rough and scholars debate it. For a teacher, English has several standard varieties, and Nigerian English has its own systematic rules.

keyPoints: Language is a rule-governed, creative system of arbitrary symbols shared by a community.
Linguistics describes language as it is used; it does not prescribe rules.
The core levels are phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics.
Naming the level of a learner’s error helps a teacher correct it purposefully.
Sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, historical linguistics and applied linguistics link language study to other questions.
English has many standard varieties; Kachru’s inner, outer and expanding circles is a rough, debated model.

en.title: English Phonetics and Phonology
en.short: Speech organs, IPA, phonemes and allophones, syllables, stress, rhythm, intonation, and transcription practice.

sections.heading: Speech organs and sounds
sections.text: Phonetics studies how speech sounds are made and described; phonology studies how sounds work as a system in a language. Speech starts with air from the lungs. The vocal folds may vibrate (voiced) or not (voiceless). Above the larynx, the pharynx, mouth and nose shape sound. The tongue, lips, teeth, alveolar ridge, hard palate and soft palate are the main articulators. Consonants are described by voicing, place and manner: /p/ is voiceless, bilabial, plosive; /z/ is voiced, alveolar, fricative. Vowels depend on tongue height, backness and lip rounding.

sections.heading: Phonemes, allophones and IPA
sections.text: A phoneme is a sound that can change meaning: /p/ and /b/ contrast in “pin” and “bin”. An allophone is a variant that does not change meaning, such as aspirated [tʰ] in “top” and unaspirated [t] in “stop”. The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) gives one symbol per sound. English consonants include /p b t d k ɡ tʃ dʒ f v θ ð s z ʃ ʒ h m n ŋ l r j w/. Common vowel symbols are /iː ɪ e æ ɑː ɒ ɔː ʊ uː ʌ ɜː ə eɪ aɪ ɔɪ əʊ aʊ ɪə eə ʊə/. These follow a reference accent such as RP; other accents, including GA and Nigerian English, differ.

sections.heading: Syllables, stress and tune
sections.text: A syllable has a nucleus, usually a vowel, with optional onset and coda: “cat” is /kæt/ (onset /k/, nucleus /æ/, coda /t/). Stress is prominence given to a syllable by loudness, length and pitch; “record” (noun) is /ˈrekɔːd/ and “record” (verb) /rɪˈkɔːd/. Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch across an utterance; it can show a question, list or finished statement.

sections.heading: Transcription and learners
sections.text: Transcribe simple words: ship /ʃɪp/, think /θɪŋk/, measure /ˈmeʒə/. When explaining pronunciation, say whether a sound is voiced, where the tongue or lips are, and give a minimal pair such as /ʃɪp/ and /sɪp/. In a Nigerian classroom, some learners may use [t] for /θ/ or [d] for /ð/, and vowel length may differ from RP. Compare accents calmly, teach the syllabus target, and do not mock local speech.

keyPoints: Speech sounds are shaped by airflow, vocal fold vibration and articulators such as the tongue and lips.
A phoneme contrasts meaning, while an allophone is a variant that does not.
IPA symbols give a consistent way to write English sounds, but reference accents vary.
A syllable has a nucleus and may have an onset and coda; stress makes a syllable prominent.
Rhythm and intonation use stress and pitch to carry meaning.
Teach pronunciation by describing voicing and place, using minimal pairs, and respecting local accents.

en.title: English Morphology and Syntax
en.short: Morphemes, inflection, derivation, word classes, phrases, clauses, sentence types and simple sentence analysis.

sections.heading: Words and morphemes
sections.text: Morphology studies how words are built. A morpheme is the smallest unit that carries meaning or grammatical function. Free morphemes stand alone (teach, book); bound morphemes must attach (-er, -s). Inflection adds grammatical information without changing the word class: book becomes books (plural), mark becomes marked (past). Derivation makes a new word, often changing class: teach becomes teacher (verb to noun), happy becomes unhappy (adjective to adjective with opposite meaning). English has a small set of inflectional suffixes and many derivational ones.

sections.heading: Word classes and phrases
sections.text: Syntax studies how words combine into phrases and sentences. Word classes group words by form and function: noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, determiner, preposition, conjunction. A phrase is a group of words built round a head. In 'the young teacher', teacher is the head of a noun phrase; young is an adjective modifying it. 'Marked the scripts’ is a verb phrase with marked as head and the scripts as object. Prepositional phrases begin with a preposition: 'in the classroom'.

sections.heading: Clauses and sentences
sections.text: A clause contains a subject and a verb that carries tense, called a finite verb. 'The teacher marked the scripts’ is a main clause. A phrase alone does not make a clause. Sentence types by purpose: declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request), exclamative (exclamation). By structure: simple (one main clause), compound (two or more main clauses joined by and, but, or), complex (main clause plus subordinate clause, e.g. 'He left because the lesson ended').

sections.heading: Analysing and teaching
sections.text: Take 'The young teacher marked the scripts quickly.' Subject: the young teacher (noun phrase). Predicate: marked the scripts quickly (verb phrase). Verb: marked; object: the scripts (noun phrase); adverbial: quickly. Morphology: teacher = teach + -er (derivation); scripts = script + -s (inflection); marked = mark + -ed (inflection). This kind of analysis gives teachers precise language for explaining errors, for example a missing third-person -s in 'she write', and helps learners move from words to phrases to clauses. Teach labels only after meaning and use are clear.

keyPoints: A morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit; free morphemes stand alone and bound morphemes attach.
Inflection adds grammatical information without changing word class; derivation makes a new word and often changes class.
Word classes include noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, determiner, preposition and conjunction.
A phrase is built round a head; a clause needs a subject and a tensed verb.
Sentence types by purpose are declarative, interrogative, imperative and exclamative; by structure simple, compound and complex.
Sentence analysis labels subject, predicate, verb, object and adverbial, and gives teachers precise language for grammar feedback.

en.title: Semantics and Pragmatics
en.short: Word meaning, sense and reference, sense relations, ambiguity, speech acts, implicature and context.

sections.heading: Meaning and reference
sections.text: Semantics studies literal meaning in language; pragmatics studies meaning in use. A word’s sense is its place in the language system, while reference is what it points to in a situation. “My uncle” and “the man in the blue shirt” can refer to the same person but have different senses. Words also carry connotation, the feelings they suggest. “Cheap” can mean low in price, but it can also suggest poor quality.

sections.heading: Sense relations
sections.text: Synonymy means sameness or near sameness of sense: “begin” and “start” are close, but not always interchangeable. Antonymy means opposite meaning. “Hot” and “cold” are gradable, with “warm” between; “alive” and “dead” are complementary, with no middle. Hyponymy is a class relation: a rose is a hyponym of flower, and flower is the superordinate. “Rose” and “tulip” are co-hyponyms. These relations help learners organise vocabulary, but context decides which word fits.

sections.heading: Ambiguity
sections.text: Ambiguity arises when a form has more than one meaning. Lexical ambiguity affects a word: “bank” can mean a river bank or a financial bank. Structural ambiguity affects a phrase: “old men and women” can mean old men plus women, or old men plus old women. Punctuation, stress and context usually resolve it. Teachers should notice ambiguity in reading passages and exam questions.

sections.heading: Pragmatics and context
sections.text: Pragmatics explains how speakers mean more than the words say. A speech act is an action done by speaking: “I promise to come” promises; “Can you open the window?” often requests. The literal question about ability is not the main point. Implicature is an implied meaning. “Some students passed” often suggests not all passed, though it does not say so. Context, shared knowledge and politeness shape interpretation. “It is cold in here” may be a request to close a window. Meaning therefore depends on who speaks, to whom, where and why.

keyPoints: Semantics studies literal meaning; pragmatics studies meaning in use.
Sense is a word’s place in the language system; reference is what it points to.
Synonymy is near sameness, antonymy is opposition, and hyponymy is a class relation.
Ambiguity can be lexical, as with bank, or structural, as with old men and women.
A speech act is an action performed by speaking, such as promising or requesting.
Implicature is an implied meaning, and context decides how an utterance is understood.

en.title: Introduction to Literary Studies
en.short: Prose, poetry and drama; plot, character, setting, theme, metre, imagery; and close reading.

sections.heading: Three genres
sections.text: Literature is studied through genres, which are recognised kinds of writing. Prose is ordinary continuous writing; prose fiction includes the novel and short story. Poetry arranges language in lines and stanzas, and often uses rhythm, metre and rhyme. Drama is written to be performed, so it uses dialogue, stage directions, acts and scenes. A genre is a guide, not a fixed box: some works mix forms.

sections.heading: Story elements
sections.text: Fiction and drama share elements. Plot is the arranged sequence of events, with causes and consequences. Character is a person represented in the text; a protagonist is the main character, and conflict is the struggle that drives action. Setting is the time, place and social world. Theme is a central idea the text explores, such as loyalty or power; it is not a simple moral. The narrator tells a prose story, and point of view is the position from which it is told.

sections.heading: Poetry and imagery
sections.text: In poetry, metre is a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables; rhythm is the broader movement of sound. A stanza is a group of lines. Imagery is language that appeals to the senses, often through metaphor (a direct comparison) or simile (a comparison using like or as). Tone is the speaker’s attitude. These terms help you describe how a poem makes meaning, not just what it says.

sections.heading: Close reading
sections.text: Close reading means examining a short passage slowly. Ask: which words are chosen, in what order, with what images and tone? Support each claim with evidence from the text. For example: “The bus coughed twice and died at the junction.” The verbs “coughed” and “died” personify the bus (give it human qualities), making it seem frail; “junction” suggests a pause. The effect may be weary humour. This reading describes the language; it does not reduce the line to a lesson about punctuality.

keyPoints: The main literary genres are prose, poetry and drama, and works can mix them.
Plot, character, setting and theme are elements of story; theme is an idea explored, not a moral.
Poetry uses line, stanza, rhythm and metre; imagery appeals to the senses through figures such as metaphor and simile.
Drama is written for performance and uses dialogue, stage directions, acts and scenes.
Close reading supports interpretation with evidence from word choice, order, imagery and tone.
A literary reading describes how the text makes meaning; it does not reduce the text to a moral lesson.

en.title: Language Acquisition and Learning
en.short: First-language acquisition, second-language learning, four theory families and classroom implications.

sections.heading: Acquisition and learning
sections.text:
Acquisition is the natural, largely unconscious growth of a language through exposure and use, as when a child learns a first language. Learning, in Krashen’s influential distinction, is conscious study of rules, such as memorising a grammar table. The distinction is useful but debated; classrooms mix both.

First-language acquisition usually needs no formal teaching. Second-language learning often follows a first language and may happen in school. In Nigeria, many learners acquire a home language and learn English as a second language.

sections.heading: Four theory families
sections.text:
Behaviourists see language as habit: children imitate, repeat and receive praise or correction, so reinforcement shapes speech. This explains routines but not new sentences.

Innatists, led by Chomsky, argue that humans have an innate language capacity, often called a language acquisition device, and universal grammar. Input matters, but the mind supplies the system. Interactionists stress communication: teachers provide input, ask questions and negotiate meaning when understanding breaks down. Sociocultural theory, from Vygotsky, sees language as learned through social participation. Mediation (learning through others and language), the zone of proximal development (what a learner can do with help but not alone) and scaffolding (temporary support) are central.

sections.heading: Classroom implications
sections.text:
English teachers can use all four views. Provide rich, comprehensible input through stories, listening and reading. Plan interaction: pair work, role play, information-gap tasks and open questions.

Scaffold with models, sentence frames and examples. Teach grammar and vocabulary explicitly, but link rules to meaningful use and give feedback on meaning and form. Respect learners’ home languages as resources. In multilingual classes, explain clearly and check understanding often.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text:
Mr Adeyemi teaches a JSS 2 English class in Ibadan. His aim is the past tense.

He reads a short story about a market day. Pairs retell it using frames such as “Yesterday I went...”. He listens, recasts errors gently (repeating what the learner said in the correct form), then asks learners to compare examples and state the rule. Finally they write three sentences about their weekend. The lesson combines input, interaction, scaffolding and explicit focus, not repetition alone.

keyPoints: Acquisition is natural and largely unconscious, while learning is conscious study, though the distinction is debated.
Behaviourism explains habit and repetition but not how learners produce new sentences.
Innatism says humans have an innate language capacity and universal grammar.
Interactionism and sociocultural theory stress communication, negotiation of meaning, the zone of proximal development and scaffolding.
English classrooms should combine comprehensible input, interaction, scaffolding and explicit grammar linked to use.
Respect learners’ home languages and check understanding in multilingual classes.

en.title: Educational Psychology for Teachers: Development, Learning and Learner Differences
en.short: How development, learning theories, motivation and learner differences shape English teaching.

sections.heading: Development and learning
sections.text: Educational psychology studies how people develop and learn, and how teachers use that knowledge. Human development covers physical, cognitive, social and emotional change. Piaget described stages of cognitive development; Vygotsky stressed social interaction and the zone of proximal development (ZPD), the gap between what a learner can do alone and with help. In English lessons, this means matching tasks to learners’ current thinking and giving temporary support.

sections.heading: Learning theories
sections.text: Behaviourism treats learning as a change in observable behaviour caused by stimuli and consequences. Reinforcement is a consequence that makes a behaviour more likely: praise after a good answer is positive reinforcement; removing a disliked task can be negative reinforcement. Punishment aims to reduce behaviour. Cognitivism studies attention, memory and processing. Constructivism says learners build new knowledge from prior knowledge; social constructivism adds interaction. Scaffolding is temporary help, such as a model paragraph, sentence starters or guided questions, which the teacher gradually removes. Metacognition is thinking about one’s own thinking: planning, monitoring and evaluating. It helps students plan an essay, check comprehension and revise.

sections.heading: Motivation and differences
sections.text: Motivation is the force that starts and sustains effort. Intrinsic motivation comes from interest; extrinsic motivation comes from rewards or pressure. Learners differ in prior knowledge, first language, vocabulary, working memory, confidence, anxiety and special educational needs. Learning preferences are often discussed, but evidence that matching teaching to them improves learning is weak. Teachers should differentiate tasks, offer choice, build belonging and give clear feedback. In English, a mixed class may read one story with different support: a glossary and audio for some, an inference question for others.

sections.heading: Classroom case
sections.text: In an invented Nigerian junior secondary class, Mr Bello teaches a short story. He begins with a picture and prediction task, models one paragraph, then lets pairs answer with sentence starters. He praises specific effort, not just ability. He asks learners to mark where they were confused and what strategy helped. This combines scaffolding, reinforcement and metacognition, and respects learner differences.

keyPoints: Human development includes physical, cognitive, social and emotional change, and tasks should match the learner’s current level.
Behaviourism explains learning through consequences; reinforcement increases a behaviour and punishment aims to reduce it.
Scaffolding is temporary support, such as models and sentence starters, that is gradually removed.
Metacognition means planning, monitoring and evaluating one’s own learning.
Motivation can be intrinsic or extrinsic, and learner differences include prior knowledge, language, confidence and special needs.
In English lessons, clear modelling, specific praise, differentiated support and metacognitive strategies help all learners.

en.title: Curriculum Foundations
en.short: Curriculum definitions, aims and objectives, models, hidden curriculum, syllabus and scheme of work, evaluation.

sections.heading: What curriculum means
sections.text: A curriculum is the whole plan of learning that a school or programme intends. It includes aims, content, teaching approaches, materials and assessment. In teacher education, it often means the official national or institutional document, but writers also use it for everything learners experience. A syllabus is narrower: it lists the topics and texts for one subject or course. A scheme of work divides the syllabus into teachable units across a term or year, with sequence and time. These are levels of planning, not rivals.

sections.heading: Aims and objectives
sections.text: Aims are broad, long-term intentions, such as helping learners use English confidently for study and work. Objectives are specific, observable statements of what learners should do by the end of a lesson or unit. Good objectives name a behaviour and, where possible, a condition and a standard. For example: 'By the end of the lesson, students will write a 120-word formal letter with correct layout and three linking words.' This is an invented example, not an official standard.

sections.heading: Models and hidden curriculum
sections.text: Curriculum models are structured ways of designing a curriculum. The objectives model associated with Ralph Tyler starts from stated objectives, then selects learning experiences, organises them and evaluates whether objectives were met. The process model associated with Lawrence Stenhouse values open, reflective inquiry and teacher judgement more than fixed outcomes. The hidden curriculum is unwritten learning from routines, rules, teacher example and school culture: punctuality, obedience, gender expectations, or which languages are valued. It can support or contradict the official curriculum.

sections.heading: Evaluation and teacher role
sections.text: Curriculum evaluation is the judging of a curriculum’s design, implementation and results, using evidence such as learner work, teacher feedback and test data. It can be formative, to improve a programme while it runs, or summative, to judge it at the end. Teachers interpret an official curriculum rather than merely transmit it. A teacher in Kano may adapt examples to local texts while keeping skills and standards. Adaptation must be recorded and justified, and requirements checked.

keyPoints: A curriculum is the whole planned learning experience; a syllabus lists subject topics and a scheme of work sequences them for teaching.
Aims are broad intentions, while objectives are specific and observable.
Tyler’s objectives model begins with stated objectives; Stenhouse’s process model values teacher judgement and inquiry.
The hidden curriculum is unwritten learning from routines, rules, teacher example and school culture.
Curriculum evaluation uses evidence to improve or judge a curriculum.
Teachers interpret an official curriculum, adapting it to learners while keeping required standards and recording changes.

en.title: Introduction to English Education
en.short: Aims and history of English as a school subject, language with literature, the teacher’s role and reflective practice.

sections.heading: English as a subject
sections.text:
English as a school subject is the planned study of the English language and its literature: reading, writing, speaking, listening, grammar, vocabulary and literary texts. English as a medium of instruction is different: it is the language used to teach other subjects. A country may use English as a subject only, or as both subject and medium. In Nigeria, English is a compulsory school subject and also a medium of instruction at later stages; policy details change, so check current official guidelines.

Aims include communicative competence (the ability to use English well in situations), literacy, literary appreciation, critical thinking and cultural awareness. Its history in many African and Asian countries is tied to colonial education, which promoted English for administration. After independence, countries kept English but reshaped its aims for national needs.

sections.heading: Language with literature
sections.text: Integrated teaching means teaching language and literature together rather than as separate subjects. A poem gives language for studying rhythm, vocabulary and tone. Grammar and reading lessons give students tools to understand literary texts. The aim is not decoration but mutual support. A class reading a short story can study past tense through the narrative and discuss character and theme. This integration is common in English education degrees.

sections.heading: Teacher and reflection
sections.text:
The English teacher plans lessons, models good language, guides discussion, gives feedback and encourages reading. Professionalism means acting with integrity, keeping subject knowledge current, following the school’s code of conduct and joining professional bodies. In Nigeria, teachers register with the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN); other countries have their own bodies.

Reflective practice means thinking about your teaching to improve it. A cycle is: teach, observe or record, ask what worked, then change one thing. Case: Mr Adeyemi, a new teacher in Ibadan, notices his students rarely speak. He records a lesson and sees he answers his own questions. He plans pair work and waits longer, then checks whether more students speak. Reflection is evidence-based adjustment, not blame.

keyPoints: English as a school subject is the planned study of English language and literature; English as a medium of instruction is the language used to teach other subjects.
Aims of English as a subject include communicative competence, literacy, literary appreciation, critical thinking and cultural awareness.
The subject’s history in many African and Asian countries is linked to colonial education, later reshaped after independence.
Integrated teaching links language and literature so each supports the other.
The English teacher plans, models language, guides discussion, gives feedback and encourages reading.
Reflective practice uses evidence from your teaching to adjust one thing at a time; professionalism includes ethics, registration and continuing development.

en.title: Teaching Listening and Speaking
en.short: Listening and speaking methods, pronunciation, dialogue, debate, drama, presentation, oral assessment and large classes.

sections.heading: Listening first
sections.text: Listening is understanding speech, not just hearing it. Teach oral comprehension through pre-listening (context and key words), while-listening (gist, then detail tasks) and post-listening (discussion or transcript work). Use bottom-up work, such as recognising sounds and word boundaries, and top-down work, such as predicting from context. Grade the task, not only the text. A short recorded dialogue, played twice, supports note-taking.

sections.heading: Speaking practice
sections.text: Speaking develops from controlled to free practice. Controlled practice gives models and repetition; free practice asks learners to use language for a real purpose. Dialogue and role play build turn-taking. Debate teaches argument, answering the other side and polite disagreement. Drama uses scripted or improvised scenes to build fluency, voice and confidence. Presentation teaches structure, linking phrases and audience awareness. In a large class, use pair and group work, roles and a time limit. Case: Mr Okafor’s 64 students prepare two-minute dialogues in pairs, then four pairs perform while others use a checklist.

sections.heading: Pronunciation
sections.text: Pronunciation teaching aims at intelligibility, being understood by listeners, not copying one accent. Teach sounds that affect meaning, word stress, sentence stress and rhythm. Minimal pairs, words that differ by one sound, such as ship and sheep, help learners hear and produce contrasts. Use modelling, choral repetition, individual repetition and quick correction. Multilingual learners can compare English sounds with their languages, but never mock an accent. Record short samples so learners hear progress.

sections.heading: Assessment and inclusion
sections.text: Assess oral skills with clear criteria: fluency, accuracy, pronunciation, interaction and task achievement. Use a rubric, a score guide, and share it before the task. Formative assessment, ongoing checking, includes observation, peer feedback and self-recording. Summative assessment, the final judgement, may be an oral exam, dialogue, debate or presentation. For reliability, use two assessors or recorded samples and compare scores. In multilingual classes, allow planning in a shared language before English performance. For large classes, rotate speaking groups, train student monitors and assess a sample deeply rather than every learner in one lesson.

keyPoints: Listening comprehension is taught in pre-, while- and post-listening stages with graded tasks.
Speaking moves from controlled practice to free, purposeful communication.
Pronunciation teaching targets intelligibility: sounds, stress, rhythm and minimal pairs.
Dialogue, debate, drama and presentation each develop different oral skills.
Oral assessment needs shared criteria and moderation for reliability.
Large multilingual classes work best with pair and group tasks, clear roles and planned support.

en.title: Teaching Reading and Comprehension
en.short: Reading skills, comprehension questions, intensive and extensive reading, vocabulary and lesson stages.

sections.heading: Reading skills and strategies
sections.text:
Reading is active. Readers use bottom-up skills, such as recognising words, and top-down skills, such as using background knowledge to predict meaning. Key strategies include skimming, reading quickly for the main idea; scanning, looking for a specific detail; predicting, guessing what comes next; and inferring, working out meaning not stated directly.

Guessing meaning from context means using surrounding words to understand an unknown word. Teachers model strategies, give practice, then ask learners how they worked out an answer.

sections.heading: Intensive and extensive
sections.text:
Intensive reading is close study of a short text. Learners read for detail, examine vocabulary and sentence patterns, and answer questions. Extensive reading means reading a lot of easy material for meaning and pleasure, often outside class. It builds fluency, vocabulary and confidence.

Reading for pleasure is free voluntary reading: learners choose texts, with no test attached. A class library and graded readers, books written at controlled levels of difficulty, support it. The two overlap, but pleasure reading stresses choice and enjoyment.

sections.heading: Lesson stages
sections.text:
Plan three stages. Pre-reading activates schema, existing knowledge, through pictures, titles or questions, and pre-teaches words needed for the task. While-reading sets a purpose: skim for the main idea, scan for details, or complete a table. Post-reading checks understanding, then uses the text for vocabulary and speaking or writing. Teach vocabulary through texts by noticing words in context, giving a definition, and recycling them later.

Example: Mr Adeyemi in Ibadan uses a passage on market day. Pre-reading: predict from the title and pre-teach bargain. While-reading: skim for the main idea, then scan for prices. Post-reading: discuss the market and write sentences with bargain.

sections.heading: Questions and difficulties
sections.text:
Comprehension questions move from literal questions, which ask for stated facts, to inferential questions, which ask what the writer implies, and evaluative questions, which ask for judgement. Reading difficulties include slow word recognition, limited vocabulary, unfamiliar background knowledge, poor fluency and anxiety.

Use graded texts, repeated reading, pair reading, glossaries and clear tasks. Do not test every text; some reading should be for enjoyment.

keyPoints: Reading combines bottom-up word recognition with top-down use of background knowledge.
Skimming, scanning, predicting and inferring are strategies that teachers should model and practise.
Intensive reading studies a short text closely; extensive reading builds fluency through large amounts of easy material.
Reading for pleasure is voluntary, chosen reading without a test.
A reading lesson has pre-reading, while-reading and post-reading stages, each with a clear purpose.
Comprehension questions should move from literal to inferential and evaluative, and difficulties need support.

en.title: Teaching Writing and Composition
en.short: Process and genre approaches, paragraph and essay structure, planning lessons, models, feedback and fair assessment.

sections.heading: Process and genre
sections.text: The process approach treats writing as recursive: planning, drafting, revising, editing and publishing. Prewriting gathers ideas for a purpose and audience; drafting gets meaning down; revising reshapes content; editing corrects spelling and punctuation. The genre approach teaches a text type’s social purpose, such as a report, argument or letter, and its typical structure and language features. It moves from model analysis to joint construction to independent writing. Process builds fluency; genre builds control of public forms.

sections.heading: Paragraphs and essays
sections.text: A paragraph develops one main idea. A topic sentence states it; supporting sentences explain or illustrate. Unity means every sentence belongs; coherence means ideas are linked clearly. An essay has an introduction stating the topic and thesis, body paragraphs developing separate points, and a conclusion drawing them together. Teach spelling and punctuation explicitly and through proofreading. Punctuation guides reading: full stop, comma, question mark, apostrophe and quotation marks. Students should use a dictionary.

sections.heading: Planning and models
sections.text: Plan a writing lesson around purpose, audience and outcome. Activate ideas, show a model, guide analysis, then give supported practice before independent writing. Models help when students identify features and then write their own; copying is not the aim. Case: a Lagos teacher plans a complaint letter lesson. Students compare two model letters, identify audience and purpose, mark paragraphs, then draft a letter to a fictional supplier. The teacher notes common problems for a mini-lesson.

sections.heading: Feedback and assessment
sections.text: Give feedback while students draft. Focus on two or three priorities linked to the lesson, such as clear topic sentences or correct apostrophes. Use self and peer review with simple checklists. Correct selectively; too much red ink discourages. Assess with a rubric covering content, organisation, language and mechanics, and show it before writing. Mark against stated criteria, not handwriting or personal taste. Moderate with a colleague for consistency. Allow revision, because writing improves through rewriting.

keyPoints: The process approach treats writing as recursive, not a single linear act.
The genre approach teaches a text type’s purpose, structure and language features through models.
A clear paragraph has a topic sentence, supporting sentences and unity.
An essay usually has an introduction with a thesis, body paragraphs and a conclusion.
Feedback should be focused, selective and given while students can still revise.
Fair assessment uses stated criteria or a rubric and moderation, not personal taste.

en.title: Teaching Grammar and Vocabulary
en.short: Inductive and deductive grammar teaching, communicative practice, error correction, vocabulary choice and recycling.

sections.heading: Deductive and inductive
sections.text: Deductive teaching gives the rule first, then practice. It is quick and suits complex or irregular forms. Inductive teaching gives examples first and the learners work out the rule; it is slower, but the rule tends to stick, because the learners have noticed the pattern themselves. Guided discovery sits between the two: the teacher asks questions that lead the class to the rule. Choose by the difficulty of the rule and the time you have.

sections.heading: Practice and correction
sections.text: Practice moves from controlled to free: a substitution drill, then a task where the grammar carries real meaning, such as an information gap, where one learner has information the other needs. Correct selectively. In accuracy work, correct at once; in fluency work, note errors and return to them later. A recast repeats the learner’s sentence correctly; elicitation asks the learner to say it again. In written work, mark two or three recurring errors, not every one.

sections.heading: Choosing vocabulary
sections.text: Select words by frequency, usefulness and the learners’ needs, not from a long list. Teach each word with form, meaning and use: "reliable" is an adjective meaning able to be trusted to do what is expected, for people or things. Depth beats breadth: eight to ten words taught well. Recycling means meeting a word again in a new context at increasing intervals, such as after a day, a week and a month; without it, most new words are lost.

sections.heading: A lesson sequence
sections.text: A 40-minute JSS3 lesson on the present perfect for experience. Warm-up (5 min): "Have you ever eaten suya?" Presentation (10 min): six example sentences on the board; pairs sort them into experience and finished time, then state the rule. Practice (15 min): a "find someone who" task. Production (7 min): pairs report two findings. Close (3 min): correct three errors you noted, and recycle five words from last week’s set.

keyPoints: Deductive teaching states the rule first; inductive teaching lets learners find it from examples.
Guided discovery uses teacher questions to lead learners to the rule.
Practice should move from controlled drills to free, meaning-focused tasks.
Correct selectively: immediate in accuracy work, delayed in fluency work.
Choose vocabulary by frequency and usefulness, and teach form, meaning and use together.
Recycle new words at spaced intervals or they are quickly forgotten.

en.title: Teaching Literature: Poetry, Prose and Drama
en.short: Approaches to teaching poetry, prose and drama, selecting texts, lesson planning and assessing response.

sections.heading: Selecting texts and planning
sections.text:
Choose texts that suit the students’ age, language level and cultural setting, and are available in class sets. A text should offer something to interpret, not just a simple moral. Consider length, vocabulary and background.

Plan a literature lesson in three stages: before reading, during reading and after reading. State one or two objectives, such as interpreting imagery or comparing characters. Prepare questions that invite evidence, not recall. For example, instead of "What happened next?", ask "Why does the writer use short sentences here?"

sections.heading: Reader response and close reading
sections.text:
Reader response treats meaning as something the reader builds from the text and their own experience. It values personal reaction, but it must be disciplined by evidence from the text. Close reading is the careful study of words, images, structure and form. Teach students to notice a detail, explain its effect and link it to the whole. Use both: begin with response, then move to close reading.

For example, a teacher in Ibadan reads a poem about a market. Students first say what they feel, then find the words that create that feeling.

sections.heading: Poetry, prose and drama
sections.text:
For poetry, read aloud and discuss sound, rhythm, line breaks and imagery. For prose, study character, setting, narrative voice and plot. For drama, use performance: read parts aloud, stage a scene, or discuss staging and gesture. Performance makes dialogue and conflict concrete.

Discussion should follow: think-pair-share, small groups or whole-class talk. In all three, ask students to support ideas with quotations.

sections.heading: Assessing response
sections.text:
Assess interpretation, not only plot recall. Use open questions that ask students to explain how a text works, such as "How does the writer make the ending surprising?" Mark with a rubric that rewards a clear claim, relevant evidence and explanation.

Include oral discussion, short written responses and creative tasks, such as writing a missing scene. Give feedback on reasoning. Avoid tests that only ask for plot facts.

keyPoints: Choose texts that offer something to interpret and suit students’ level and context.
Plan literature lessons in three stages: before, during and after reading.
Reader response values personal reaction, but close reading grounds it in evidence from the text.
Teach poetry through sound and imagery, prose through character and voice, drama through performance.
Discussion and performance help students explore meaning together.
Assess interpretation with open questions and rubrics that reward claims supported by evidence, not plot recall.

en.title: Children’s and Young Adult Literature
en.short: Genres, book selection, age and culture, and classroom use to build reading culture.

sections.heading: Genres and features
sections.text: Children’s literature is written for younger readers, often up to about twelve; young adult (YA) literature is written for teenagers. Common genres include picture books, where words and pictures together make meaning; chapter books and novels; folklore and fairy tales; fantasy; realistic fiction; poetry; and non-fiction. Features vary by age. Picture books use simple text and strong images. Chapter books use short chapters and simple vocabulary. YA novels often explore identity, friendship, family and social issues. Good books still have clear characters, a strong plot and language suited to the reader.

sections.heading: Choosing books
sections.text:
Selection uses several criteria. Age appropriateness means the book’s language, length, themes and emotional demands fit the reader’s development, not only their class. Interest matters: a book a learner chooses is more likely to be finished. Readability means the text is challenging but not frustrating. Cultural relevance means learners can see their own lives and also meet lives beyond them; check for stereotypes and accurate detail. Quality means convincing writing, memorable language and respect for the child.

In a Nigerian junior secondary class, Mrs Adeyemi rejects a novel that mocks rural speech, then chooses one with a city girl and a village cousin. She reads two pages aloud before deciding.

sections.heading: Using books in lessons
sections.text:
In language lessons, a short text can supply vocabulary, sentence patterns and writing models. In literature lessons, use read-aloud, prediction, literature circles (small groups discussing one book), role play and response journals. Ask open questions about character, choice and language. Do not turn every reading into a test.

To build a reading culture, keep a classroom library, give regular free reading time, let learners recommend books, and involve parents. A book club and simple book talks help. The aim is pleasure first, with analysis growing from it.

keyPoints: Children’s literature is written for younger readers and YA literature for teenagers; genres include picture books, novels, folklore, fantasy, poetry and non-fiction.
Age appropriateness depends on language, length, themes and emotional demands, not class level alone.
Choose books for interest, readability, cultural relevance, quality and freedom from stereotypes.
Use read-aloud, literature circles, role play and response journals in language and literature lessons.
Build reading culture with a classroom library, free reading time, book talks and family involvement.
Do not make every reading a test; pleasure and choice support lasting reading.

en.title: African Literature in English: Themes, Contexts and Teaching
en.short: Themes, forms and contexts of African literature in English, with representative texts and classroom approaches.

sections.heading: Oral roots
sections.text: African literature in English grows beside a strong oral tradition: folktales, proverbs, praise poetry, songs and drama performed before an audience. Oral forms shape written style through direct speech, repetition, riddles and a narrator who addresses listeners. Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) uses Igbo proverbs and communal scenes; Wole Soyinka’s play The Lion and the Jewel draws on dramatic performance. Teach learners that oral tradition is living material, not just background.

sections.heading: Colonial context
sections.text: Colonialism is the political and economic control of one territory by another power. In much of Africa Britain ruled colonies and introduced English through mission and government schools. Postcolonial literature, writing after and about colonial rule, responds to that experience: it questions colonial versions of history, explores independence and its disappointments, and debates the use of English. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o's A Grain of Wheat (1967) treats Mau Mau, the Kenyan uprising against British rule, and independence in Kenya; he later chose to write in Gikuyu, his Kenyan mother tongue. Ayi Kwei Armah’s The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born (1968) shows post-independence disillusionment.

sections.heading: Themes and forms
sections.text: Common themes include tradition and change, identity, gender, migration, corruption and community. Forms include the novel, short story, drama and poetry. Avoid reducing every text to "culture clash". Ask who narrates, whose language is used, what symbols recur and what historical pressures shape the plot. Tsitsi Dangarembga’s Nervous Conditions (1988) examines gender and colonial education in Zimbabwe; Buchi Emecheta’s The Joys of Motherhood (1979) questions motherhood and city life in Nigeria.

sections.heading: Teaching the texts
sections.text: With school learners, begin with story and character before history. A teacher in Enugu, in an invented case, asks learners to collect a proverb from home and compare its work in Things Fall Apart. Use role-play for drama, debate for contested choices, and short writing in a character’s voice. Give historical notes briefly and accurately. Let learners test the text: does it idealise the village, blame colonialism alone, or show internal conflict? End with a clear paragraph using evidence.

keyPoints: African literature in English draws on oral forms such as proverbs, folktales and praise poetry.
Colonialism and mission education shaped the language and institutions of this literature.
Postcolonial writing questions colonial history and explores independence and its disappointments.
Major themes include tradition and change, identity, gender, migration and corruption.
Discuss texts through narrative voice, language, symbol and historical context, not culture clash alone.
With learners, start with story, use local oral material, and require evidence-based interpretation.

en.title: Survey of English Literature
en.short: Periods, genres and representative texts from Old English to the present, with selection advice.

sections.heading: Periods and genres
sections.text: A literary period is a label for writing produced in a span of time, shaped by history, language and taste. Genre means a kind of writing, such as epic, lyric, sonnet, drama, satire or novel. Period borders are convenient, not fixed, and dates differ between syllabuses. English literature is usually studied as a sequence from Old English to the present, but curricula differ on whether it means the literature of England or literature in English. Check the syllabus before choosing texts.

sections.heading: Early to eighteenth
sections.text: Old English writing includes the epic Beowulf and shorter elegies. Middle English includes Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales and mystery plays. The Renaissance, roughly the sixteenth century in England, brought Shakespeare’s plays and sonnets, Spenser’s The Faerie Queene and Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus. The seventeenth century includes Donne’s metaphysical poetry and Milton’s Paradise Lost. Restoration and eighteenth-century writing includes satire by Swift and Pope, and the rise of the novel in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding.

sections.heading: Romantic to modern
sections.text: Romantic writing, late eighteenth to early nineteenth century, stresses imagination and feeling; examples are Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lyrical Ballads and Keats’s odes. Victorian literature, from 1837 to 1901 in the UK, includes Dickens, the Brontës, George Eliot and Tennyson. Modernism, mainly early twentieth century, experiments with form in Woolf, Joyce, Eliot and Yeats. Post-1945 writing includes Beckett’s Waiting for Godot and later novelists and poets. These labels overlap and are debated.

sections.heading: Choosing texts
sections.text: For secondary school, choose texts that suit age, language level, length and the local exam syllabus. Use extracts from long works and give historical glosses. A concrete case: a teacher may introduce Shakespeare through Sonnet 18, a short poem, to teach imagery and Elizabethan context before a full play. Explain that a text speaks from its period but is not merely a mirror of it. Avoid explicit content, and check availability and cost.

keyPoints: Period labels such as Romantic or Victorian are convenient and overlap; dates vary by syllabus.
Genre terms include epic, lyric, sonnet, drama, satire and novel.
Old English, Middle English, Renaissance, seventeenth-century, Restoration and eighteenth-century texts form the early survey.
Romantic, Victorian, modernist and post-1945 writing form the later survey.
Select secondary texts by age, language, length, exam syllabus and availability.
Historical context should illuminate a text, not replace close reading.

en.title: Sociolinguistics and World Englishes: Variation, Standards and Classrooms
en.short: English variation by region, group and context, world Englishes, and teaching standard English with respect.

sections.heading: Variation and varieties
sections.text: Sociolinguistics studies how language use changes with society. A dialect is a variety shared by a region or social group; everyone speaks at least one dialect. Register is the variety chosen for a situation, such as a laboratory report or a family meal. Style is a speaker’s adjustment within a register, for example becoming more formal with a visitor. Variation by region, social group and context is normal, not a sign of laziness. No dialect is linguistically inferior, though people often rank them socially.

sections.heading: Standard and world Englishes
sections.text: Standard English is the written and formal variety used in education, publishing and public administration in many places. It is a prestigious dialect, not the only correct English. Non-standard forms follow their own rules. Nigerian English is the set of English varieties used in Nigeria, with recognised features in pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar; scholars debate which features belong to a standard Nigerian English. World Englishes describes postcolonial and global varieties. Kachru’s Three Circles model groups countries as inner, outer and expanding, but it is a model, not a law.

sections.heading: Attitudes and multilingual classrooms
sections.text: Language attitudes are beliefs and feelings about a variety; they can raise or lower a learner’s confidence. A deficit view treats a home variety as wrong, which can silence students. In multilingual classrooms, code-switching means moving between languages or varieties. A teacher in Kano, for example, may let pupils discuss a poem in Hausa before writing in English. This supports thinking while keeping English as a goal.

sections.heading: Teaching with respect
sections.text: Teach the standard explicitly as a tool for public and academic life, not as a rejection of home English. Use contrastive examples: compare "I have gone" with a local form, name the context, and avoid shaming. Model standard English in your own speech and materials, and assess the target features you taught. Oral and written expectations can differ. Check national curriculum and exam policy, because accepted school norms vary by country.

keyPoints: Sociolinguistics studies how language varies by region, social group and context.
Dialect, register and style are normal dimensions of variation; no dialect is linguistically inferior.
Standard English is a prestigious variety, not the only rule-governed English.
Nigerian English and other world Englishes have recognised features; Kachru’s circles is a model, not a fixed law.
Language attitudes can support or damage learners; code-switching can be a classroom resource.
Teach standard English explicitly and respectfully, using contrastive examples and checking local policy.

en.title: English Curriculum and Lesson Planning
en.short: Reading English curriculum documents, schemes of work and writing lesson plans with clear objectives.

sections.heading: Curriculum, syllabus, scheme
sections.text: A curriculum is the overall plan of aims, content and standards for a subject or level. A syllabus is the subject breakdown: topics, learning outcomes, suggested activities and assessment. A scheme of work turns the syllabus into a term or year plan, showing what is taught each week. In Nigeria, the national curriculum is developed by the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council (NERDC) and approved through the National Council on Education; state ministries and schools adapt it. Other countries use different bodies and formats, so check the current official document.

sections.heading: Reading and sequencing
sections.text: To interpret a syllabus, list its aims, outcomes, content, suggested methods, materials and assessment. Check prerequisites and move from simple to complex. Sequence skills so that listening and speaking support reading and writing, and leave weeks for revision and tests. Example: Mr Okoro in Kaduna has 12 teaching weeks and four units. He gives two weeks to each unit (4 × 2 = 8), two weeks to revision and two to assessment, making 12 weeks. If the syllabus has more topics, he reduces unit time or asks the head of department to adjust the scheme.

sections.heading: Writing a lesson plan
sections.text: A lesson plan is a short guide for one lesson. It states the class, date, topic, duration, previous knowledge, learning objectives, materials, activities and evaluation. A learning objective says what learners will do by the end, using observable verbs such as identify, explain or write. Example: 'By the end of the 40-minute lesson, learners will be able to pick out the topic sentence in three short paragraphs, scoring at least two out of three.' Activities should move from teacher modelling to guided practice and independent work. Evaluation is a quick task that checks the objective. Keep plans flexible and note the official source.

keyPoints: A curriculum gives overall aims; a syllabus lists topics and outcomes; a scheme of work places them week by week.
In Nigeria, NERDC develops the national curriculum and the National Council on Education approves it; states and schools adapt it.
Sequence lessons from simple to complex and leave time for revision and assessment.
A learning objective should name an observable learner action and a standard.
A lesson plan should include objectives, activities and an evaluation that checks the objectives.
Curriculum documents differ by country and change, so check the current official source.

en.title: Assessment in English Education
en.short: Formative and summative assessment, test design, marking, feedback, and assessing language and literature.

sections.heading: Purposes and types
sections.text: Assessment gathers evidence about learning. Formative assessment happens during teaching. It gives feedback to learner and teacher and is usually not graded. Summative assessment happens at the end of a unit, term or course. It judges achievement against goals and often gives a grade. Both are needed: formative assessment guides the next lesson; summative assessment reports what has been learned.

sections.heading: Validity, reliability, fairness
sections.text: Validity asks whether a test measures what it claims. A grammar test that mainly tests memory of rules may be reliable but not valid for writing ability. Reliability means consistency: the same test, marked by different teachers or taken on different days, should give similar results. Fairness means items, language and conditions do not unfairly favour or disadvantage a group. Clear instructions, familiar topics and reasonable time help. Use several tasks when stakes are high.

sections.heading: Building and marking
sections.text: Start with a table of specifications, or test blueprint. It lists objectives and content, and the number of items for each. Match item types to the skill: multiple choice for coverage, short answer for explanation, essay for extended writing. Write clear instructions and prepare a marking scheme or rubric before marking. For writing, an analytic rubric might score content, organisation and language separately. Moderate a sample of scripts with a colleague. Feedback should be specific, timely and actionable. If 16 students take a quiz and 12 answer item 5 correctly, item difficulty p = 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75, moderately easy. Values near 1 are very easy; near 0 are very hard.

sections.heading: Language and literature
sections.text: Language assessment covers listening, speaking, reading, writing, grammar and vocabulary. Use tasks that match the skill: a short talk for speaking, a passage with questions for reading, a draft with revision for writing. Literature assessment asks for comprehension, interpretation and response to texts, through passage questions, essays and oral discussion. Portfolios show progress over time. After marking, group common errors and reteach them. Record results and adjust the scheme of work. External examinations differ by country and board, so check the current syllabus.

keyPoints: Formative assessment gives feedback during learning; summative assessment judges achievement at the end.
Validity means a test measures what it claims; reliability means consistent results; fairness means no unfair bias or barriers.
A table of specifications matches test items to objectives and content.
Item difficulty is p = number correct ÷ number who attempted the item; p = 12 ÷ 16 = 0.75 is moderately easy.
Mark writing with a clear rubric and moderate samples to keep marking consistent.
Use results to reteach weak areas and adjust teaching; check local syllabus and board rules.

en.title: Instructional Materials and ICT
en.short: Selecting, adapting and designing English materials, low-resource and ICT use, copyright and criteria.

sections.heading: Choosing materials
sections.text: Instructional materials are resources a teacher uses to support learning: textbooks, charts, pictures, audio, video and digital tools. ICT means information and communication technology, such as phones, radio, computers and learning platforms. Choose materials by asking whether they match the syllabus and objectives, suit learners’ age and English level, present accurate and respectful content, support the target skill, and are clear, durable and affordable. Check bias and cultural fit. An attractive material that is too hard, or leads to no practice, wastes time.

sections.heading: Adapting and designing
sections.text: Adaptation means changing a resource to fit your class without losing its purpose. You can shorten a long text, simplify vocabulary, add glosses (short explanations of hard words), localise names and examples, add pictures, or replace a task with pair work. When designing a chart, worksheet or audio, keep one main idea per item, use clear print, check spelling, and write instructions learners can follow alone. Case: Mrs Okafor in Kano has one comprehension passage for 60 students. She copies it onto a chart, pairs learners to read alternate sentences, and gives each group one question.

sections.heading: Low-resource classrooms
sections.text: Low-resource classrooms may lack textbooks, electricity, internet or a projector. Plan around what you have: the board, paper, real objects, learners’ knowledge and local radio. Make reusable materials such as flashcards and word charts. Use pair and group work so one copy serves many. Lack of technology need not stop communication: a picture, a short dialogue or a song can teach English well.

sections.heading: ICT and copyright
sections.text: Use ICT only when it improves learning. Test devices and files before class, prepare offline copies, and have a backup. Keep digital tasks short, accessible and private. Copyright is the legal right of creators over their work. Rules differ by country, and educational exceptions are limited. Use your own materials, public domain works (out of copyright), licensed copies or open educational resources (OER), whose licence states reuse rights. Do not upload a copyrighted textbook PDF to a class group. Attribute sources and seek permission when unsure.

keyPoints: Choose materials that match objectives, learners’ level and the target skill, and that are accurate, respectful and affordable.
Adapt by simplifying, shortening, localising and adding tasks or visuals without losing the learning aim.
Low-resource classes can use the board, real objects, pair work and reusable charts instead of technology.
Test ICT before class, prepare offline backups, and use it only where it improves English learning.
Copyright protects creators; rules differ by country, so use licensed, public domain or OER material and attribute it.
Do not copy or upload protected textbooks without permission or a clear legal exception.

en.title: Classroom Management for English Lessons
en.short: Routines, rules, motivation, group work, discipline and large mixed-ability English classes.

sections.heading: Purposeful management
sections.text: Classroom management is the organisation of people, time, space and materials so that learning can happen. It is not control for its own sake. A well-managed English lesson has a clear purpose, brisk transitions and all students working. The teacher plans the opening, main task and close, and prepares materials before the lesson. Management supports learning when students spend more time reading, speaking, writing and thinking, and less time waiting.

sections.heading: Routines and rules
sections.text: Routines are repeated procedures, such as entering, collecting books, forming groups and handing in work. They save time and reduce uncertainty. Rules are shared expectations, stated positively: listen while others speak, bring materials, try before asking for help. Agree a few rules and display them. Teach routines as you teach language: explain, model, practise and praise. Consistency matters more than severity. A raised hand or short countdown can bring attention back without shouting.

sections.heading: Motivation and groups
sections.text: Motivation is the reason a student engages. Intrinsic motivation comes from interest and progress; extrinsic motivation comes from praise, marks or rewards. English tasks motivate when clear, achievable and meaningful: a short debate, a letter to a real audience, a story read aloud. Group work means students learning together in pairs or small groups. Give each member a role, such as chair, writer or reporter, and set a time limit. Mixed-ability grouping can help if tasks have shared core work and extension. Monitor and correct briefly.

sections.heading: Discipline and classes
sections.text: Discipline is guidance that protects learning, not punishment. Prevent disruption through purposeful tasks and correction of problems. Use private reminders first, then consistent consequences agreed by the school. For large classes, use whole-class responses, board instructions, pair work and peer checking so every student is active. In mixed-ability classes, prepare graded questions and optional extension. For example, Mrs Okafor’s Senior Secondary class begins with short silent reading, then pair work with roles while she monitors groups.

keyPoints: Classroom management organises people, time, space and materials so learning can happen.
Routines are taught, modelled and practised until they become automatic.
Rules should be few, positive, agreed with the class and applied consistently.
Motivation is stronger when English tasks are clear, achievable and meaningful.
Group work needs roles, time limits and active monitoring.
Discipline protects learning through prevention, private reminders and consistent consequences, especially in large or mixed-ability classes.

en.title: Inclusive Education in English Teaching
en.short: Inclusion, differentiation, accessible materials, struggling readers and teachers’ legal duties.

sections.heading: What inclusion means
sections.text:
Inclusive education means all learners, including those with disabilities, different home languages, genders and abilities, learn together in English lessons with support. It is not treating everyone identically; it is removing barriers so that each learner can take part and succeed.

Integration expects the learner to fit an unchanged class. Inclusion changes teaching, materials and the classroom. Barriers can be physical, such as poor lighting, linguistic, such as unexplained vocabulary, or social, such as mocking an accent.

sections.heading: Differentiation and materials
sections.text:
Differentiation is planned adaptation of content, process, product and environment so each learner works at a suitable level. In English this may mean shorter texts with glossaries, a choice of written or oral response, extra time, or extension tasks.

Accessible materials use clear fonts, strong contrast, plain language, captions, audio and screen-reader-friendly files. Universal design for learning (UDL) builds multiple ways of representing information, engaging learners and letting them show what they know. In an Ibadan class, all study one poem, but the teacher gives a recorded reading, a glossary and a choice of paragraph or poster.

sections.heading: Reading and language support
sections.text:
Struggling readers need early identification and explicit support: pre-teaching vocabulary, modelled and paired reading, shorter chunks, extra time or audio. Multilingual learners should use their home language to plan or clarify while learning English.

Teachers should value all languages, avoid punishing accents, and teach academic English. Gender matters: choose texts that avoid stereotypes, share speaking turns fairly and challenge sexist remarks. Mixed ability is normal, so plan open tasks with support and challenge built in.

sections.heading: Duties and limits
sections.text:
Teachers have legal and ethical duties to avoid discrimination, make reasonable accommodation (fair changes that remove barriers), keep learners safe and treat them with dignity. Law and provision vary by country; examples include the Equality Act 2010 in Great Britain and the Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018 in Nigeria.

Check national policy and school rules. Record needs, seek specialist help, and do not disclose a diagnosis unnecessarily.

keyPoints: Inclusion changes teaching and the classroom so all learners can take part, rather than expecting learners to fit an unchanged class.
Differentiation adapts content, process, product and environment to a learner’s level.
Accessible materials and universal design for learning give multiple ways to receive information and show learning.
Struggling readers and multilingual learners need explicit vocabulary support, extra time and respect for home languages.
Teachers should avoid gender stereotypes, share participation fairly and challenge sexist remarks.
Legal duties and provision vary by country, so check current national policy and school rules.

en.title: Professional Ethics for Teachers
en.short: Teachers’ ethical duties: care, fairness, confidentiality, relationships, authority and codes.

sections.heading: Duty of care
sections.text: Professional ethics is the study of what teachers ought to do, not only what rules allow. Duty of care means protecting learners from harm and supporting their wellbeing. It covers safe classrooms, respectful language and adequate preparation. Case: a pupil says she is being harmed at home. Listen calmly, do not promise secrecy, write down what was said, and follow the school’s safeguarding procedure. Do not investigate alone.

sections.heading: Fairness and confidentiality
sections.text: Fairness means consistent treatment and marking against published criteria, without favouring relatives or private pupils. Case: two essays look alike. Ask both learners to explain their work before any accusation. Confidentiality means sharing learner information only with people who need it. Case: a colleague asks about a learner’s medical condition. Refer the colleague to the designated staff member. Safety may require disclosure under school policy and law.

sections.heading: Relationships and authority
sections.text: Professional relationships need clear boundaries. Avoid being alone with a learner in a closed room, and avoid romantic, financial or family ties that could affect judgement. Responsible use of authority means never using marks, punishment or access to opportunities to pressure learners. Case: a learner asks for a private talk after class. Use a visible space and tell a colleague. Corporal punishment is banned in many countries and restricted in others; check local law and school policy.

sections.heading: Codes of conduct
sections.text: A code of conduct sets out expected behaviour and complaint procedures. Codes differ by country and institution, and they change. In Nigeria, the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) regulates registered teachers. Read your own code and ask a senior colleague when unsure. Report breaches through the proper channel; whistleblowing means reporting wrongdoing to protect learners.

keyPoints: Professional ethics guides teachers beyond legal minimums.
Duty of care requires protecting learners and following safeguarding procedures.
Fairness means consistent, criteria-based treatment; confidentiality limits sharing learner information.
Keep professional boundaries and never use authority for personal gain.
Codes of conduct differ by country and institution; know and follow your own.
Report breaches through proper channels to protect learners.

en.title: Microteaching and Teaching Practice
en.short: The microteaching cycle, peer observation, feedback, reflective journals and school placement conduct.

sections.heading: The microteaching cycle
sections.text: Microteaching is a scaled-down lesson: a student teacher teaches a small group of peers for a few minutes, usually to practise one skill such as explaining or questioning. The microteaching cycle has stages: plan a short lesson with one clear objective; teach it; observe; receive feedback; reflect; then re-plan, re-teach and get feedback again. The re-teach matters because it turns feedback into practice. A useful micro-lesson states the objective, learner activity, materials and timing.

sections.heading: Feedback and peer observation
sections.text: Peer observation means watching a colleague teach with a clear purpose. An observation instrument is the form used to record evidence: a checklist of behaviours, a rating scale, a running record of what teacher and learners do, or a schedule focused on one question, such as how often learners speak. Feedback should be specific, based on evidence and about behaviour, not personality. For example, Amina teaches a ten-minute micro-lesson on question tags. Her peer notes that she asked twelve questions but waited only one second after each. In feedback they agree she will wait three seconds and re-teach. This is a small, checkable target.

sections.heading: The teaching practice placement
sections.text: The teaching practice placement is a block of supervised teaching in a real school, usually in the later years of the degree. The student teacher works with a school mentor and a university supervisor. Duties include preparing schemes of work and lesson plans, teaching classes, keeping records, assessing learners and taking part in school life. Responsibility should grow gradually. Ask for the school’s rules and timetable early, and follow the national and school policies that apply.

sections.heading: Reflection and conduct
