sections.text: A reflective journal is a regular written record of what happened in a lesson, why it happened and what to try next. It is not a mere diary: it links evidence to action. Professional conduct includes punctuality, suitable dress, respect for learners and staff, confidentiality, and following school rules and the law of the country. Record observations honestly, and do not discuss learners outside a professional need.

keyPoints: Microteaching is a short, scaled-down lesson used to practise one teaching skill.
The cycle is plan, teach, observe, give and receive feedback, reflect, then re-plan, re-teach and get feedback again.
Peer observation uses an instrument such as a checklist or running record to gather evidence.
Feedback should be specific, evidence-based and focused on behaviour that can be changed.
A teaching practice placement is supervised school teaching with a mentor and university supervisor.
Reflective journals link lesson evidence to future action, and professional conduct follows school rules and national law.

en.title: Research Methods in English Education
en.short: Research designs, topics, literature review, sampling, data collection, analysis, ethics and project reports.

sections.heading: Designs and topics
sections.text: Research is a planned, systematic search for answers. A research design is the plan for collecting and analysing evidence. Quantitative designs use numbers, often to test a hypothesis, which is a testable statement. Qualitative designs use words to explore meaning and experience. Mixed methods combine both. Choose a small, clear topic you can finish, such as how secondary teachers use group reading in large classes. Narrow it by setting, participants and question.

sections.heading: Reading and sampling
sections.text: A literature review is a critical summary of what earlier studies found, showing the gap your study addresses. Read journal articles, textbooks and official reports; record full references. Sampling means choosing a part of the population, the whole group your study is about. In simple random sampling every member has an equal chance of selection. In purposive sampling you choose people for a clear reason, such as experienced English teachers. State your sample size and how you chose it.

sections.heading: Collecting and analysing
sections.text: Common instruments are questionnaires, interviews, observation schedules and tests. Validity means an instrument measures what it claims; reliability means it gives consistent results. Pilot, or trial, the instrument on a few people first. Simple analysis can use percentages and means. Example: 40 pupils take a reading test and 30 reach the pass mark. The pass rate is 30 ÷ 40 × 100 = 75%. If four scores are 50, 60, 70 and 80, the mean is (50+60+70+80) ÷ 4 = 260 ÷ 4 = 65. Report what the numbers show without overclaiming.

sections.heading: Ethics and report
sections.text: Research ethics protect people. Seek informed consent, explain the purpose, allow withdrawal, keep names confidential or anonymous, avoid harm, and get institutional approval. Do not invent or alter data. A small project report, such as your final-year project, usually has a title, abstract (a short summary), introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion, references and appendices. Write plainly, link results to your question, and state limitations. Follow your department’s current format and submission rules.

keyPoints: Research design is the plan for collecting and analysing evidence.
Quantitative studies use numbers, qualitative studies explore meaning, and mixed methods use both.
A literature review summarises existing studies and identifies the gap your study addresses.
Simple random sampling gives every population member an equal chance; purposive sampling selects people for a clear reason.
Validity means measuring what is claimed; reliability means giving consistent results.
Percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100; mean = sum of scores ÷ number of scores; follow research ethics and your department’s report format.

en.title: Theories of Second Language Acquisition
en.short: Cognitive, interactionist and sociocultural theories of second language acquisition, with critiques.

sections.heading: Input and interaction
sections.text: Krashen’s monitor model claims that we acquire a second language by understanding input slightly beyond our current level, which he called i+1, provided the affective filter, a block caused by anxiety or low motivation, is low. The interaction hypothesis (Long) holds that negotiation for meaning, where learners signal non-understanding and rephrase, makes input comprehensible and highlights form. Swain’s output hypothesis adds that speaking and writing push learners to notice gaps. Schmidt’s noticing hypothesis states that attention to form is necessary for intake, the language actually taken in.

sections.heading: Cognitive processing
sections.text: Information-processing theories treat second language learning as skill acquisition. Declarative knowledge, knowing rules, becomes procedural, using them fluently, through practice, then automatic (Anderson; DeKeyser). McLaughlin’s attention-processing model describes the same shift: controlled processing is slow and effortful, while automatic processing frees working memory. Aptitude and working memory predict how fast learners progress. Transfer from the first language and explicit instruction also shape the route.

sections.heading: Sociocultural perspectives
sections.text: Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory sees learning as social first and internalised later. The zone of proximal development is the distance between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help; scaffolding is that temporary support, withdrawn as competence grows. Languaging, talking or writing about language, helps learners gain control. Dynamic assessment measures learning potential rather than a fixed score.

sections.heading: Critique and classroom use
sections.text: Critics note that Krashen’s i+1 cannot be measured independently, and that sociocultural studies are often small and weak at prediction. Cognitive models can underplay identity and emotion; Norton’s notion of investment describes learners who are motivated yet withdraw. In one classroom case, a teacher in Ibadan sets an information-gap task so pairs must negotiate meaning, then gives brief focus on form, a short look at the past tense inside the meaning-focused lesson, then asks for a written recount. Curriculum aims and medium-of-instruction policy draw on these theories and on bilingual education research. In Nigeria, policy favours the mother tongue as medium of instruction in the early primary years before a shift to English, but practice varies and the rules change, so check the current National Policy on Education.

keyPoints: Krashen’s monitor model links acquisition to comprehensible input and a low affective filter, but its constructs are hard to test.
The interaction hypothesis holds that negotiation for meaning makes input comprehensible and draws attention to form.
Swain’s output hypothesis and Schmidt’s noticing hypothesis stress production and attention as drivers of development.
Cognitive skill-acquisition theory describes declarative knowledge becoming procedural and then automatic with practice.
Sociocultural theory explains learning through the zone of proximal development, scaffolding and languaging.
Classroom research supports meaning-focused tasks with brief focus on form, but no single theory explains all learning.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods in English Education
en.short: Designing a research project or dissertation: questions, methods, sampling, analysis, ethics and appraising research.

sections.heading: Questions and designs
sections.text: A research project or dissertation starts with a research question: a focused, answerable question naming the population, setting and issue. A qualitative design explores meanings and experiences, often through interviews or classroom observation. A quantitative design measures variables, which are factors that can take different values, often through tests or questionnaires. A mixed methods design combines both, either to explain results or to broaden understanding. The design must fit the question.

sections.heading: Sampling and instruments
sections.text: Sampling is choosing participants. Probability sampling gives every member of a defined population a known chance of selection, so findings can generalise. Non-probability sampling does not support statistical generalisation; purposive sampling, for example, selects information-rich cases. Sample size depends on design, question and analysis; no single rule fits all. Instruments are the tools used to collect data: questionnaire, interview guide, observation schedule or test. Pilot the instrument, then check validity (does it measure the intended construct?) and reliability (are scores consistent?). Invented case: a student studies 40 teachers’ feedback practices with a 20-item questionnaire. If 10 items are unclear in the pilot, revise them before the main study.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text: Analysis follows the design. Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics, such as means and percentages, and, where justified, inferential tests, which estimate whether patterns are likely beyond the sample. Qualitative analysis often uses thematic analysis: coding transcripts, grouping codes into themes, and checking interpretations against the data. Mixed methods analysis integrates the two strands in a table or narrative. Ethics require research ethics committee approval, informed consent (participants understand and agree freely), voluntary participation, anonymity (no names or identifying details are collected), confidentiality (identities are protected) and secure data storage. Extra care is needed with minors and sensitive classroom data.

sections.heading: Proposal and appraisal
sections.text: A proposal states the background, question, literature review, design, sample, instruments, analysis plan, ethics, timeline and limitations. Judge published research by asking whether the question, design, sample, instruments, analysis and claims align. Check for bias, missing information and overgeneralisation. A strong study reports enough detail for another researcher to understand and repeat it.

keyPoints: A research question must be focused, answerable and matched to the design.
Qualitative designs explore meaning; quantitative designs measure variables; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; purposive sampling selects information-rich cases.
Pilot instruments and check validity and reliability before the main study.
Analysis must fit the design, and ethics approval and informed consent are required.
Appraise published research by checking alignment among question, design, sample, instruments, analysis and claims.

en.title: Critical Literacy and Multimodality: Reading Power in Words and Images
en.short: Critical literacy, multimodality, power in texts, and teaching reading, literature and writing.

sections.heading: Critical literacy
sections.text: Critical literacy treats reading as an act of questioning, not only decoding. It asks whose interests a text serves, whose voices are included or missing, and how language positions the reader. Paulo Freire linked reading the word to reading the world; Norman Fairclough showed how grammar and word choice carry power. The four resources model of Peter Freebody and Allan Luke names four reader roles: code breaker, text participant, text user and text analyst. Critical literacy stresses the analyst role. A reader may accept a text, negotiate with it or resist it.

sections.heading: Multimodality
sections.text: Multimodality is the study of how meaning is made through several modes at once. A mode is an organised resource for meaning, such as speech, writing, image, colour, layout, gesture or sound. Gunther Kress and Theo van Leeuwen’s social semiotics, the study of how people use signs and resources to make meaning in society, treats images as having a grammar: gaze, angle, framing, salience and colour direct attention and create relations with the viewer. Each mode has affordances, meaning its own possibilities and limits. Digital media are multimodal and interactive, so readers also navigate links, menus and moving images.

sections.heading: Teaching implications
sections.text:
These views change English teaching. Reading lessons ask who produced a text, for whom, and what it leaves out. Literature teaching examines power in character, setting and voice, and compares print with film or graphic versions. Writing becomes design: students compose posters, digital stories or blogs, choosing modes for an audience, then explain their choices.

In a JSS3 class in Ibadan, Mr Adeyemi’s pupils analyse a bottled-water advertisement. They note the smiling child, the bright kitchen and the logo, then ask who can afford the water and whose daily life is absent. They redesign the poster for a public tap, using words and images to argue for safe water.

keyPoints: Critical literacy asks how texts position readers and whose interests they serve.
Multimodality studies meaning made through modes such as image, layout, colour and sound.
Social semiotics offers a visual grammar of gaze, angle, framing and salience.
The four resources model names code breaker, text participant, text user and text analyst.
Teaching should ask students to analyse image-text relations and to redesign texts for real audiences.
Digital media add interactivity, so critical reading includes navigation and design choices.

en.title: Language Policy and Planning in Education
en.short: How language policy shapes medium of instruction, multilingualism and English teaching.

sections.heading: Policy and planning
sections.text: Language policy is a set of decisions about which languages are used, taught and assessed. Language planning is the organised effort to carry out those decisions. Status planning sets a language’s role and prestige; corpus planning develops vocabulary, spelling and grammar; acquisition planning decides who learns what, when and how. In education, policy sets the medium of instruction (MOI), the language used to teach subjects, and the place of English.

sections.heading: Medium and multilingualism
sections.text: Mother-tongue education uses a child’s home language as the MOI. Multilingualism is the normal use of more than one language. Bilingualism may be additive, adding a second language while supporting the first, or subtractive, where a dominant second language gradually replaces the first. English as a second language (ESL) means English is learned where it has an official or everyday role, not only in class. English as a foreign language is learned where it is not widely used outside school.

sections.heading: Country cases
sections.text: Nigeria’s National Policy on Education recommends the mother tongue or language of the immediate community as MOI in early primary, with English taught as a subject and used increasingly later. Implementation varies by state, teacher supply and materials. Tanzania uses Kiswahili as the primary MOI and English mainly from secondary school, so English teachers face a sharp transition. South Africa’s language-in-education policy promotes multilingualism and home-language learning in early grades, but many schools move to English early. Policy and practice often differ.

sections.heading: Effects on English teaching
sections.text: Policy affects English teaching through time allocation, starting age, examinations, textbooks and teacher language proficiency. A late transition can limit exposure to academic English; an early transition can weaken mother-tongue learning if support is poor. For example, five English lessons of 40 minutes a week give 5 × 40 = 200 minutes, or 3 hours 20 minutes, of planned English weekly. Teachers must align methods and assessment with the official MOI and use learners’ other languages as a resource where policy allows.

keyPoints: Language policy sets which languages are used, taught and assessed; planning is how those decisions are carried out.
Status, corpus and acquisition planning are three common dimensions of language planning.
Medium of instruction is the language used to teach school subjects.
Mother-tongue education can support early learning, while an early transition to English can weaken it if support is poor.
Nigeria’s policy recommends early mother-tongue or community-language MOI with English taught as a subject, but implementation varies.
Policy shapes English teaching through time, starting age, examinations, materials and teacher proficiency.
